extracted.intended_audience: SNL fans and general entertainment readers interested in viral comedy clips
extracted.subtask_description: A Newsweek list article that catalogs fifteen Saturday Night Live sketches that were cut from the live broadcast but later became popular online, with short descriptions and view counts. The page is a pop-culture roundup rather than a how-to or formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut decision: dress rehearsal audience response
rubrics_metrics.description: After a dress rehearsal, staff make decisions on which sketches to cut based on whether they were working or not for the dress audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural standard explains why sketches are removed from the live broadcast — editors/producers judge a sketch's effectiveness by the dress rehearsal reaction. Example context from the page: many of those 'cut-for-time' sketches are comedy gems despite being removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-show distribution of unaired sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: NBC frequently posts cut sketches on its YouTube channel or NBC's site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice guidance about preservation and audience reach: even if a sketch is unaired, it may be published online by the network for further exposure. Examples on the page include multiple cut sketches that were later made available online and gained traction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online view counts as indicator of a sketch's popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists view counts (e.g., '13 M views', '7.7M views') next to each sketch to indicate which cut sketches became online sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page treats high viewership numbers and memeification (e.g., 'Alan' turning into a meme) as evidence of success post-broadcast; use of views and social spread is implied as a metric for measuring impact.
